column2: Ephraim's complaint about not being called and fierce contention remain; the question addresses Gideon's omission at departure for war.
Gideon's comparative question uses Ephraim's gleanings and Abiezer's vintage, retaining the agricultural contrast rather than supplying an explanatory victory paraphrase.
The Lord's delivery of Oreb and Zeeb explains Gideon's comparison; both they stopped and their spirit relaxed remain, with the timing tied to his words.
Gideon and three hundred cross Jordan fainthearted and hungry; the selected hunger and diminished-heart description are not replaced by weary yet pursuing.
The bread request rests on hunger while Gideon pursues the two named Midianite kings; the plural loaves are represented collectively as bread in this provisioning context.
Succoth's rulers question whether the two kings' hand is already in Gideon's hand before supplying his army; the singular shared hand idiom remains.
Not so precedes the conditional future divine delivery and Gideon's threat with wilderness thorns and barkonnim; the opaque second implement remains transliterated.
column3: Barkonnim requires lexical and textual review; neither briers nor a threshing instrument is asserted as its resolved meaning.

column2: Penuel receives the same speech and gives the same response as Succoth; the repeated comparison remains without inventing a new reply.
Return in peace conditions the future demolition of this tower; the specific tower and timing remain.
About fifteen thousand remain at Karkar from the eastern camp, while one hundred twenty thousand sword-drawers have fallen; the approximate remnant and exact stated losses stay distinct.
The tent-dwellers' route lies east of Nabeth opposite Zebah; Gideon strikes while the camp is confident. Selected geography is not replaced with another name sequence.
Flight, pursuit, seizure of both named kings and wiping out their whole camp remain; exetripsen is not softened into mere camp alarm.
Gideon son of Joash returns by the ascent of Ares; the selected ascent/name is not converted into a time-before-sunrise phrase.
Plural they capture a young man, singular he questions him, and the young man records seventy-seven rulers/elders for them; the number and pronoun shifts remain.
Gideon presents Zebah and Zalmunna with Behold, recalls the reproach and quotes the hand/bread question, now describing his men as weary; hungry in 8:5 is not harmonized to this quotation.
Both rulers and elders are taken, with repeated tearing by wilderness thorns and barakēnim applied to Succoth's men; the selected verb is not changed to taught.
column3: Barakēnim differs in form from barkonnim at 8:7 and remains distinct pending lexical/apparatus review.

column2: Penuel's tower is demolished and the city's men killed; both actions remain without softening or adding a motive.
Where are the Tabor victims is followed by repeated likeness clauses, you, them and the appearance of kings' sons; the difficult repetition remains.
column3: The singular/plural referents and relationship of resembling them to resembling you remain unresolved; the speech is not compressed into they looked like you.

column2: Change They were my brothers to They are my brothers for explicit present eisin, retaining the ongoing kinship assertion. Sons of my mother, the Lord-lives oath and the unreal survival condition remain.
column3: The past aorist with an in the apodosis is rendered would not kill in the prospective execution setting; its temporal force requires fuller syntactic review.

column2: Jether is Gideon's firstborn; the command to kill fails because the boy is afraid and young. Both reasons and the undrawn sword remain.
The kings ask Gideon himself to attack, state the man/strength comparison, and are killed; crescents are then taken from camel necks.
column3: Fall upon is a contextual violent sense of meet in the execution request, not a claim that the verb always means kill.

column2: Israel requests rule among us by Gideon and plural sons because of rescue from Midian; no grandson is added.
Gideon refuses for himself and singular my son, then assigns rule to the Lord; the change from plural sons in the request is retained.
A request for each man's spoil earring follows, with many gold earrings explained by the Ishmaelite identity; the singular request is naturally one thing in English.
column3: The final they refers contextually to the defeated people whose ornaments became spoil; the source pronoun itself is not replaced with an explicit ethnic army subject.

column2: The emphatic gift promise, singular he spreading his cloak and each man's gold earring remain; no plural cloak-spreading actor is supplied.
One thousand seven hundred gold shekels excludes sirōnes, small necklaces enphōth, royal purple cloaks and camel gold collars; all categories and both exclusion phrases remain.
column3: Sirōnes and enphōth remain unresolved. Called supplies an English appositional link for the latter, not evidence that its identification with the adjacent necklaces is certain.

column2: Gideon's ephod is set in Ephrathah, where all Israel prostitutes itself after it and it becomes a stumbling block to him and his house; the selected place and sexual metaphor remain.
Midian is put to shame, no longer lifts its head, and the land rests forty years in Gideon's days; the head image and duration remain.
Jerubbaal son of Joash returns to his house; the narrative name change is retained without replacing it with Gideon.
Seventy sons from his loins are explained by many wives; loins represents the source's bodily descent idiom rather than omitting it.
The Shechem concubine also bears a son, named Abimelech by the implicit male actor; her status remains distinct from the preceding wives.
Gideon dies in good old age and is buried in Joash's tomb at Ephrathah of the father of Abiezri; the selected paternal place formulation remains.
column3: The geographical and genealogical attachment continues the unresolved wording in 6:11,24; no Abiezrite/Ophrah normalization is imposed.

column2: Gideon's death leads to renewed prostitution after Baalim and setting Baal-berith in a covenant to be their god; both name and explicit covenant remain.
Israel forgets the Lord who rescued them from every surrounding enemy; the negative remembering and complete rescue scope remain.
Failure of mercy toward Jerubbaal/Gideon's house contrasts with all his goodness toward Israel; both names and the reciprocal relationship remain.
